items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Colon cancer rates in the U.S. are on the rise for the first time in 20 years. Here’s who’s most at risk
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ ✏️

If you’re overdue for a colonoscopy, let this be your reminder: Colorectal cancer rates are increasing for pretty much everyone.

While word has gotten out about rising colorectal cancer rates among younger adults, a new study found that rates are climbing across all age groups up to the age of 69. Researchers from the University of Chicago found that the overall incidence rate for this type of cancer—the second-leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S.—rose for the first time in more than 20 years, according to a study published earlier this week in NEJM Evidence.

The age-adjusted incidence rate of colorectal cancer rose from 36.7 per 100,000 people in 2022 to 38.3 in 2023, the study authors found. By comparison, the incidence rate in 2000 was 55.2. The incidence rate among people between the ages of 45 and 49 rose nearly 13% from 2019 to 2023, the sharpest increase among any age group—although that’s likely driven by more people in this cohort undergoing screenings. In 2021, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force lowered the recommended age for a first screening from 50 to 45.

“That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do—it’s catching cancer earlier,” Caitlin Murphy, the lead author of the study and a professor of pediatrics and public health sciences at the University of Chicago, said in a statement. 

But earlier screening doesn’t explain why the incidence rate is also rising among older adults between the ages of 65 and 69, as they’re about 80% up to date with screenings and historically benefitted from this detection method. The results suggest that unknown risk factors may be offsetting the previous gains from screening—and the study’s authors say they still need to understand why that’s happening.

“In terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now causing it to increase in older people as well,” Murphy said.

THEORIES FOR THE ROOT CAUSE

Finding that root cause of colorectal cancer remains the biggest mystery for researchers to unravel. Earlier this year, new evidence showed that colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among men and women under the age of 50. Meanwhile, nearly 160,000 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer this year, including both colon cancer and rectal cancer, according to estimates from the American Cancer Institute.

Theories for what causes colorectal cancer are wide ranging. A recent study found that faster biological aging could be a factor that’s associated with an increased risk of several early-onset cancers, including colorectal cancer. The authors of this latest study plan to explore another possible culprit: environmental chemical exposures.

Working with a toxicologist from Emory University, the team from the University of Chicago will measure thousands of environmental exposures to see which ones warrant further research, then test those chemicals on organoids, which are specialized models that can grow colons in a dish.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

items.title: [sootoday.com] Canadian bill would bar MAID for mental illness alone, allow advance requests
items.content_html: Canada’s Liberal government introduced Bill C-41 on Oct. 27 to indefinitely exclude people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness from medical assistance in dying (MAID). It would also allow advance requests from people diagnosed with incurable illnesses that could later leave them unable to consent. The bill must pass both chambers before March 17, 2027, when the scheduled expansion to mental illness as a sole qualifying condition is due to take effect. Justice Minister Sean Fraser said he wants the House of Commons to pass it before Parliament’s December break. Advance requests would not trigger MAID automatically: two independent practitioners would have to confirm eligibility, the person would have to be suffering intolerably and in irreversible decline, and any demonstrated refusal or resistance would stop the procedure. Provinces and territories would decide whether to allow advance requests and provide MAID under them. The bill follows a parliamentary committee’s recommendation to exclude mental illness indefinitely, citing unresolved questions about safe and consistent assessment.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Former DOGE staffers say they just hacked Anthropic in less than 12 hours
items.content_html:
A cybersecurity firm run by former members of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) says it has broken into internal data and messaging systems at Anthropic. Perhaps even more surprising, though, is its claim that it did so in less than 12 hours.

The startup is called Cathedral, and it classifies itself as an AI-driven cybersecurity firm with a focus on military applications. In July, Cathedral closed a $160 million funding round that valued the company at $1.4 billion, with investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital.

How Cathedral got inside Anthropic

Cathedral says it was able to penetrate Anthropic by taking advantage of vulnerabilities in business software the company uses—the same software used by many other businesses. Among the data it claims to have accessed were meeting transcripts, salary information, job offers, and Slack messages discussing its AI models.

“The fact that weaknesses in ordinary enterprise software can compromise the infrastructure of even the most advanced organizations should be a wake-up call for every company in America,” a report from Cathedral read, according to The Washington Post.

Anthropic has a program inviting outside cybersecurity companies to test its systems, so this would qualify as a white-hat hacking incident. The AI giant confirmed Cathedral had accessed “a limited set” of its systems and said it has since shut down those access points. The company also said that Cathedral spent multiple days unsuccessfully trying to break into its software directly before turning its attention to third-party business tools.

Despite that, Cathedral’s apparent success in breaching Anthropic has raised eyebrows in Washington, D.C. One unnamed official told the Post: “If a bunch of kids who have just started a company can do this, then potentially, the Chinese aren’t far behind.”

Anthropic’s rocky relationship with the Trump administration

The Trump administration and Anthropic have had a rocky relationship for some time. Donald Trump labeled Anthropic a “radical left, woke company” earlier this year and ordered all federal agencies to cut ties and stop using its products. The Pentagon designated the company a “supply-chain risk,” prompting a lawsuit.

In its S-1 paperwork leading up to its IPO, Anthropic warned potential investors about the potential impact of that tension: “The political environment and our engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action.”

Cathedral’s ties to Trump

Cathedral’s founders include several people with close ties to the Trump administration. Among the former DOGE staffers running the company are Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, Marko Elez, and Jack Stein.

Kliger also previously served as the Pentagon’s chief data officer and was reportedly involved in the department’s skirmish with Anthropic. Elez was forced to resign from DOGE after he was linked to tweets containing phrases such as “normalize Indian hate,” “You could not pay me to marry outside of my ethnicity,” and “Just for the record, I was racist before it was cool.” (Musk rehired him despite the controversy.)

The company is reportedly developing AI software it hopes to sell to the Pentagon to bolster the military’s cybersecurity capabilities, guarding against and launching attacks on adversaries like China. Reuters also reports that Cathedral is looking to acquire a data center or to partner with one for dedicated computing power.

The midterm elections could complicate those ambitions, though. Should Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives or Senate, they could closely scrutinize contracts awarded to companies run by founders with especially close ties to Trump, potentially slowing Cathedral’s progress.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut
items.content_html: The secret to aging more slowly may be hiding in your gut. Scientists discovered that certain gut bacteria are strongly linked to how quickly the body ages, with microbial differences accounting for about 15% of the variation in biological aging rates. Some bacterial species were associated with slower aging, while others were linked to accelerated aging.
